title: Pronunciation Foundations: Read What You Hear
description: Learn the sound rules carried by Hawaiian spelling so the words you rehearse in your head match what you are more likely to recognize in speech.

sourceReview.notes: Pronunciation rules are taken from UH and the modern Reference Grammar. Learner help describes Hawaiian sound cues rather than replacing Hawaiian spelling with English-style respelling.

activities.support: Hawaiian vowel qualities are much more stable than English spelling.
soundNotes: a — like the a in above
e — like e in bet
i — like the final y in city
o — like o in sole, but without the English off-glide
u — like oo in moon, without an added off-glide
activities.languageNote: Use these as sound anchors, not as an English respelling system.

activities.support: A kahakō marks a longer vowel and that vowel is stressed.
soundNotes: ā — longer a; compare the reference sound to a in far
ē — longer e; reference comparison ay in pay
ī — longer i; reference comparison ee in see
ō — longer o
ū — longer u
Vowels with kahakō are somewhat longer and are always stressed
activities.languageNote: Do not treat a kahakō as decoration. It changes pronunciation and can distinguish words.

activities.instruction: Treat the ʻokina as a consonant.
activities.support: The ʻokina is part of the Hawaiian alphabet.
soundNotes: The ʻokina is a glottal stop.
UH compares it to the break between the two parts of English “oh-oh.”
Because it is a consonant, it can separate adjacent vowels into different syllables.
activities.languageNote: When you see ʻ, do not silently skip it.

activities.instruction: Learn the shape of a Hawaiian syllable.
activities.prompt: Every Hawaiian syllable ends in a vowel.
activities.support: This makes written Hawaiian unusually informative once you know the sound system.
soundNotes: A Hawaiian syllable is a vowel by itself or a consonant followed by a vowel.
Two ordinary consonants do not occur together inside a Hawaiian syllable.
The ʻokina counts as a consonant.
A Hawaiian word ends in a vowel.
activities.languageNote: Use the written vowels to help you hear syllable boundaries instead of compressing the word using English habits.

activities.prompt: Stress is part of sounding natural.
activities.support: The reference grammar gives predictable default stress rules, with longer words forming accent groups.
soundNotes: In words shorter than four syllables, stress normally falls on the second-to-last syllable.
If the final syllable has a kahakō, that final long vowel receives the strongest emphasis.
Longer words may have more than one accent group.
A stressed Hawaiian syllable is somewhat louder, longer, and often higher in pitch.
activities.languageNote: These are useful reading rules, but fluent speech still needs listening practice.

activities.instruction: Do not flatten Hawaiian vowel sequences into English diphthongs.
activities.prompt: ai · ae · ao · au · ei · eu · oi · ou
activities.support: The second vowel retains more vowel quality than an English off-glide.
activities.sourceText: ai ae ao au ei eu oi ou
soundNotes: The reference grammar groups ei, eu, oi, ou, ai, ae, ao, and au as rising diphthongs.
The first element is stressed.
The second element remains more vowel-like than the weak glide heard in many English diphthongs.
activities.languageNote: This is one reason an English-looking respelling can easily teach the wrong sound.

activities.prompt: What does a kahakō tell you?
activities.support: Choose the pronunciation consequence, not merely the visual description.
options: The vowel is longer and stressed
activities.answer: The vowel is longer and stressed
activities.explanation: The modern reference grammar describes vowels with kahakō as somewhat longer and always stressed.

activities.support: Treat it as part of the alphabet.
options: A consonant representing a glottal stop
activities.answer: A consonant representing a glottal stop
activities.explanation: UH and the reference grammar treat the ʻokina as a consonant/glottal stop.

activities.prompt: Which statement matches Hawaiian syllable structure?
activities.support: Think about how Hawaiian words are built.
options: A syllable always ends in a vowel
A syllable normally ends in two consonants
activities.answer: A syllable always ends in a vowel
activities.explanation: The reference grammar states that Hawaiian syllables always end in a vowel.

activities.instruction: Apply the sound rules to real spelling.
activities.prompt: If you see a word with both ʻokina and kahakō, what should you do?
activities.support: Choose the reading habit the app wants you to build.
options: Pronounce both cues rather than ignoring them
activities.answer: Pronounce both cues rather than ignoring them
activities.explanation: Both marks carry pronunciation information and belong to correct Hawaiian orthography.
